name: Vardhamaneeswaram, Tiruppugalur
deity: Shiva as Vardhamaneeswarar, within the Agneeswarar temple at Tiruppugalur
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung by Tirugnanasambandar
summary: Tiruppugalur, near Nannilam, is a venerable Shaiva village where the great Agneeswarar temple holds within it a second Paadal Petra Sthalam, Tiru-Pugalur Vardhamaneeswaram, sung by the child-saint Tirugnanasambandar. The town is famous for the miracle in which the lord turned ordinary bricks to gold for the saint Sundarar, and to this day those about to build a home come here to offer a brick and seek blessings. Agni, the fire-god, is said to have worshipped here to be freed from a curse.

sections.history: Tiruppugalur is an ancient Shaiva village near Nannilam, revered in the seventh-century Tevaram. Its principal temple is the Agneeswarar (Agnipureeswarar) temple, named for Agni the fire-god, who is said to have worshipped here to be freed from a curse. Uncommonly, the same complex also enshrines a distinct Paadal Petra Sthalam, Tiru-Pugalur Vardhamaneeswaram, which was glorified by the child-saint Tirugnanasambandar — so that two of the 275 Tevaram shrines are found on one sacred ground. The stonework is of the Chola period with later additions.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Dravidian complex of gopuram, prakara corridors and pillared halls. Within it the sanctum of Vardhamaneeswarar is counted as its own Paadal Petra Sthalam, alongside the main Agneeswarar sanctum. The inner precinct is rich with images — the sixty-three Nayanmars, Agni, the Pancha Linga, Appar, Vatapi Ganapati, Subramanya, Mahalakshmi and Kalasamhara among them — making the complex a compact gallery of the Shaiva pantheon.
sections.legends: The most beloved tradition is the miracle of the bricks. The saint Sundarar, needing wealth for the festival expenses of his wife Paravai Nachiyar, prayed here and slept upon a few ordinary bricks; by morning the lord had turned them to gold. From this grace comes the custom, kept to this day, by which those about to build a new house visit the temple, offer a brick to the deity and pray before laying their foundations. The temple also preserves the story of Agni worshipping Shiva here to be released from a curse, which gives the Agneeswarar sanctum its name.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham, the Margazhi observances and the annual Brahmotsavam. The association with Sundarar and with the brick miracle gives special meaning to the days honouring the Nayanmars, and the custom of offering a brick before house-building brings a steady stream of family visits through the year.
sections.experience: Tiruppugalur rewards the pilgrim with a sense of layered sanctity — two Tevaram shrines in one, a crowded precinct of saints and gods, and a living custom that ties the temple to the ordinary hope of building a home. Standing before the sanctum of Vardhamaneeswarar, visitors feel the nearness of a grace that once turned bricks to gold and still blesses new beginnings.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruppugalur is in Nagapattinam district near Nannilam, roughly 15 km from Nagapattinam and Tiruvarur; the nearest rail heads are Nannilam and Nagapattinam, with local buses and taxis to the village.
